{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01XD6PFrjw6KCKZQQ4PQq6Z2","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Eval harness — rubric, test prompts, protocol\n2\t\n3\tMeasures whether a produced BUILD PLAN actually follows the skill. Run the plan generator (with the skill) on a prompt.\n40\t2. Score each of the 10 dimensions 0–2; sum to /20.\n41\t3. Record the score and the weakest dimension.\n42\t\n43\t## With-skill vs without-skill baseline\n44\t\n45\tFor the same prompt, compare:\n46\t- **Without skill:** a plan written feature-first / by visibility. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_5qncwejhkzxtf63sumslddyglv7qqg5wdxo6m7la7jgjtq4mpzva","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Zero-downtime cloud migration of the hospital patient scheduling system\n\n## 1. Classification\n- **What:** Moving a live, in-house (or customizable) patient scheduling application and its relational database from on-prem to a HIPAA-eligible cloud. The system has HL7 links to the EHR, ADT feeds, reminder vendors, and reporting, and it must never visibly go down.\n- **Type:** Infra plus software. This is a data-migration and traffic-routing problem. It is not a rewrite.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness, meaning no lost or double-booked appointments. Compliance (HIPAA) is a close second, and availability is the third requirement.\n- **Worst failure:** Split-brain writes. On-prem and cloud both accept bookings during cutover, which causes double-booked OR or clinic slots, or appointments that silently disappear. A close second is outbound feeds firing twice, which sends duplicate SMS reminders to patients and duplicate SIU messages to the EHR.\n- **Assumptions to confirm before Phase 0:**\n  - **Vendor product?** If the system is a vendor product such as Epic Cadence or Oracle Health scheduling, the vendor's hosting program decides the migration path, and most of this plan becomes vendor-managed.\n  - **What \"without downtime\" means here:** no user-visible outage. The single write cutover still pauses writes for a few seconds (target under 30 s): they are held and then replayed, not rejected. The existing paper downtime procedures stay staffed as a safety net.\n\n## 2. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Default (chosen now) | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Consistency vs availability** | **CP, one writer.** Exactly one database is authoritative at any moment. No dual-writes, no multi-master. The cloud copy is read-only until the cutover. | **Never flip to multi-master for this system.** If availability drills fail RTO, add a cross-region warm standby. It stays single-writer. |\n| **Cutover granularity** | **One atomic write-authority switch for the whole system**, with writes held at the proxy. Shared resources (radiology rooms, surgeons, interpreters) cross department lines, so splitting writes by department would need bidirectional replication. | Flip to per-site cutover only if the Phase 1 inventory proves that a site's resources share nothing with the others. |\n| **Migration style (rehost / replatform / re-architect)** | **Replatform.** Same app code on cloud VMs or containers, with a managed DB on the **same engine** (e.g. SQL Server on-prem → Azure SQL MI or RDS SQL Server). No refactoring during the move. | Flip to rehost (lift-and-shift VMs) if licensing or OS dependencies block managed services. Re-architecting is deferred (§7). |\n| **DB engine change** | **Keep the same engine.** Same-engine CDC is far more reliable, and an engine change on top of a migration compounds risk. | Revisit after migration only if licensing cost is over budget. That becomes its own project. |\n| **Monolith vs services** | **Keep the monolith as-is.** | Extract a service (e.g. reminders) only after migration, if it limits scaling or release speed. |\n| **Sync vs async** | **Synchronous** booking writes, so the user sees a confirmed slot. **Async** CDC replication and interface fan-out over durable queues. | If replication lag p99 goes above 5 s, reads that need fresh data stay on the primary and are not served from the replica. |\n| **Build vs buy** | **Buy:** managed CDC (AWS DMS / Azure DMS / Qlik / GoldenGate), managed DB, and the existing integration engine (Rhapsody / Mirth / Cloverleaf) rehosted. **Build:** only the reconciliation checks and the cutover runbook. | Build trigger-based capture only if the CDC tool can't handle specific types (LOBs, computed columns) or the change volume. |\n| **Cloud / compliance boundary** | A provider with a **signed BAA**, an in-country region, multi-AZ, private connectivity only, and customer-managed keys. | A data-residency or state-law requirement forces the region choice. A provider refusing a BAA disqualifies it. |\n| **Identity** | **Federate to the existing hospital AD** (Entra ID / SAML). No new user store. | None. A second identity store for clinical staff is not acceptable. |\n| **Rollback model** | **On-prem stays a hot standby** after cutover, fed by reverse CDC (cloud → on-prem), for 30–90 days. | Retire it early only after the cloud cross-region DR has passed a failover test. |\n| AI gates (RAG vs fine-tune, hosted vs self-host) | N/A. The migration has no AI component. | Becomes relevant if AI features such as no-show prediction are proposed later (§7). |\n\n## 3. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n**The one real request:** a scheduler looks up *\"provider availability for Clinic X tomorrow.\"* It is served end-to-end from the cloud using real production data. Writes are not possible on this path.\n\n**Tiers crossed:**\n1. Scheduler workstation (existing client, SSO via hospital AD)\n2. On-prem reverse proxy / load balancer (F5 or NGINX). This becomes **the routing control point** for the whole migration.\n3. Redundant private link: ExpressRoute or Direct Connect, plus a backup IPsec VPN\n4. Cloud private load balancer and WAF\n5. Cloud app instance in **read-only mode**, enforced by a database login that only has `SELECT` grants\n6. Cloud managed DB replica, fed by CDC from the on-prem primary. To start, only the tables needed for this one query are replicated.\n\nThe response goes back along the same path.\n\n**Who gets real responses:**\n- 100% of matching requests are mirrored in shadow mode, and the cloud response is diffed against the on-prem response.\n- A pilot group of 3–5 IT or scheduling super-users gets the cloud response for real, using a feature flag at the proxy.\n- If the cloud path is slower than 2 s or errors, the proxy falls back to on-prem.\n\n**Day zero deploy, logging, monitoring:**\n- Infra and app deploy from Terraform/Bicep through a CI pipeline. Nothing is set up by hand.\n- A correlation ID is attached at the proxy and logged on both sides. Logs are structured and PHI-scrubbed, and sent to a SIEM covered by the BAA.\n- The dashboard shows p95 latency, error rate, CDC lag, shadow-diff rate, and proxy fallback count. Alerts go to on-call.\n- **Started now because it needs a long lead time:** passive network-flow and DB-connection capture on the on-prem DB server, so monthly and quarterly jobs show up in the Phase 1 inventory.\n\n**Exit check:**\n- A pilot user's availability lookup returns from the cloud in production.\n- The trace shows every tier, and the lag and diff metrics are visible on the dashboard.\n- The shadow-diff rate is 0 over 72 h, apart from known differences that are explained.\n\n## 4. Phases (ordered by dependency; within a phase, widest blast radius first)\n\n**Phase 0: Walking skeleton** (above)\n- Tasks, in order:\n  1. BAA signed\n  2. Landing zone with policy guardrails\n  3. Private connectivity\n  4. SSO federation\n  5. Proxy routing control point\n  6. Partial CDC\n  7. Read-only app instance\n  8. Dashboard\n\n**Phase 1: Prove the data substrate and find every dependency**\n- Unlocks: everything else. Nothing gets routed to the cloud until the data is provably identical and every consumer is known.\n- Depends on: the Phase 0 CDC path and private link working in production.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Dependency inventory.** Combine flow capture, DB login audit, interface-engine routes, and cron/SQL Agent jobs to list every reader and writer: ADT inbound, SIU outbound, reminder/IVR vendor, billing, reporting/BI, and ODBC links from Access or Excel. A missed consumer is the most likely silent failure after cutover.\n  2. **Put indirection in front of every consumer.** Every client, interface, and report must reach the system through the proxy or a DB listener/DNS alias. The cutover then becomes a routing change instead of reconfiguring 40 clients. Remove hardcoded IPs.\n  3. **Full-database CDC** with schema parity checks. Schema changes are frozen, or applied to both sides through versioned migrations.\n  4. **Continuous reconciliation:** hourly row counts plus per-table checksums, and a nightly full-hash comparison of the appointment and slot tables.\n  5. Restore a cloud backup to a scratch instance to prove point-in-time recovery (PITR) works.\n- Exit check:\n  - 14 consecutive days of full replication with lag p99 under 5 s and zero unexplained reconciliation diffs.\n  - The inventory is signed off by the interface team and department leads.\n  - 100% of consumers go through switchable indirection.\n\n**Phase 2: Rebuild integrations in the cloud, in dry-run**\n- Unlocks: moving traffic without breaking feeds to the EHR, billing, and patients.\n- Depends on: the Phase 1 inventory, plus replicated data that is proven identical.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Write-authority flag and singleton guard.** A single flag says which side is authoritative. Every outbound interface and batch job (reminders, SIU, nightly exports) checks it before acting, so the cloud **cannot** send to patients or to the EHR while on-prem is authoritative.\n  2. Run cloud outbound interfaces in **capture-only mode**. Generated HL7 SIU and reminder payloads are compared message-by-message with what on-prem actually sent.\n  3. Pre-provision the inbound ADT path to the cloud, but leave it inactive. On-prem still receives ADT, and the changes reach the cloud through CDC.\n  4. Re-point reports and BI to the cloud replica, since they only read.\n- Exit check:\n  - 7 days of outbound dry-run with a 100% match against on-prem messages.\n  - The singleton guard is verified by trying to fire a cloud job while on-prem is authoritative. It must refuse.\n  - Reports run from the cloud without a regression.\n\n**Phase 3: Move read traffic gradually**\n- Unlocks: proven cloud capacity and latency under real load before writes depend on it.\n- Depends on: Phase 2 interfaces running in parallel, and the Phase 1 reconciliation staying green.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Handle read-your-writes.** After a user writes, route that session's reads to the primary for 30 s. Also, if CDC lag goes over the threshold, the proxy sends all reads to on-prem automatically.\n  2. Load-test the cloud at 2× the observed peak, for example the Monday 08:00 booking surge.\n  3. Ramp read routing through the proxy: 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%, department by department, with automated canary analysis at each step.\n  4. Move portal \"view my appointments\" to the cloud last, because it is patient-facing.\n- Exit check:\n  - 100% of reads served from the cloud for 14 days with SLOs met (p95 under 800 ms, errors under 0.1%).\n  - The stale-read counter stays at 0 complaints and 0 detected cases.\n\n**Phase 4: Rehearse the write cutover and the rollback**\n- Unlocks: a cutover whose risk has been measured, not guessed.\n- Depends on: Phase 3 proving the cloud can carry production load.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Reverse CDC** (cloud → on-prem), built and verified in staging. This is the rollback mechanism.\n  2. **Cutover runbook as code:** the scripted sequence with go/no-go checks at every step.\n  3. **At least 3 full rehearsals and at least 1 full rollback rehearsal** on a staging environment built from IaC, using a masked clone of production data at production size. Time each one.\n  4. Define rollback triggers. Examples: booking error rate above 0.5% for 5 min, any double-booking detected, interface ACK failures, or CDC reverse lag above 60 s.\n  5. Get clinical operations sign-off. Choose a low-volume window (e.g. Sunday 02:00, avoiding month-end and holidays). Put downtime procedures and print-ready schedules on standby.\n- Exit check:\n  - The rehearsed write-hold is under 30 s, three times in a row.\n  - The rollback rehearsal restores on-prem authority in under 15 min with zero data loss.\n  - The CAB and the CMIO sign off.\n\n**Phase 5: Switch write authority**\n- Unlocks: the cloud becomes the system of record.\n- Depends on: a Phase 4 rehearsal passing at the current production versions.\n- Tasks, executed from the rehearsed script:\n  1. The proxy holds writes, with a bounded queue.\n  2. Confirm CDC lag is 0 and checksums match.\n  3. Set the on-prem DB to read-only.\n  4. Flip the write-authority flag.\n  5. Start reverse CDC.\n  6. Activate cloud ADT inbound, outbound interfaces, and batch jobs. The singleton guard turns on-prem's copies off.\n  7. Release the held writes to the cloud.\n  8. Run synthetic book/cancel transactions against a test patient.\n  9. Hold a **4-hour war-room watch**, then a 72 h heightened watch.\n- Exit check:\n  - 72 h with zero double-bookings, zero lost appointments (reconciled against reverse CDC), all interface ACKs green, and SLOs met.\n\n**Phase 6: Bake, prove DR, decommission**\n- Unlocks: retiring on-prem without losing the safety net it currently provides.\n- Depends on: a stable Phase 5 cloud primary.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Cross-region DR replica plus a real failover test.** On-prem is the only DR until this passes, so it comes first.\n  2. Keep the on-prem hot standby for 30–90 days.\n  3. Make on-prem a read-only archive and apply record-retention rules.\n  4. Decommission with NIST 800-88 media sanitization certificates.\n  5. Close out on-prem accounts, firewall rules, and circuits.\n- Exit check:\n  - The DR failover test meets RTO ≤ 1 h and RPO ≤ 5 min (targets to confirm with clinical ops).\n  - The decommission certificates are filed.\n\n## 5. Cross-cutting concerns (per phase, from the first commit)\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **0** | BAA signed; landing-zone policy guardrails; private endpoints only; CMK encryption; TLS 1.2+; AD federation; read-only DB login | Correlation IDs on both sides; PHI-scrubbed logs to SIEM; latency, error, lag, and diff dashboard; on-call alerts | All infra in Terraform/Bicep through CI; immutable app images; no console changes | Proxy falls back to on-prem on timeout or error; dual circuits plus VPN backup; the cloud path is shadow/pilot only |\n| **1** | Least-privilege CDC service account; replication over the private link only; HIPAA risk assessment updated; DB access audit logging | Reconciliation and lag metrics with SLO alerts; inventory dashboard of every consumer | Schema as versioned migrations; CDC task config in git; reconciliation queries in git | Multi-AZ cloud DB; CDC resumes from checkpoint; tested PITR restore |\n| **2** | Interface credentials in a secrets manager; HL7 over TLS/VPN; vendor endpoints allow-listed | Message-level outbound diff dashboard; interface ACK/NAK monitoring | Interface-engine routes exported to git; the write-authority flag defined in code | Durable queues with DLQs; singleton guard prevents duplicate sends; replayable message store |\n| **3** | WAF rules tuned; **external pen test before any real user traffic beyond the pilot**; portal session security reviewed | Per-route SLOs; canary analysis per ramp step; stale-read counter | Routing rules and flags as code; load-test scripts versioned | Automatic read fallback on lag or latency breach; 2× peak load test passed |\n| **4** | Access review of every cutover operator; tabletop of a PHI incident during cutover | Cutover single-pane dashboard; synthetic book/cancel probes every minute | Runbook as code; staging rebuilt from IaC with a masked production clone; rehearsal timings recorded | Reverse CDC verified; rollback rehearsed under 15 min; downtime procedures and printed schedules staged |\n| **5** | Just-in-time privileged access for the cutover window only; every cutover action logged to the SIEM | War-room dashboard; continuous double-booking detector query; interface ACK alarms | Cutover runs from the rehearsed, version-pinned script; change freeze in effect | Bounded write-hold queue; predefined rollback triggers; hot on-prem standby through reverse CDC |\n| **6** | Revoke on-prem accounts and firewall rules; NIST 800-88 sanitization; retention policy applied | DR replication lag monitoring; cost and capacity dashboards; post-migration SLO report | DR environment built from the same IaC; as-built documentation generated from code | Cross-region failover tested; scheduled game days; standby retired only after DR passes |\n\n## 6. AI layer\nN/A. This plan has no AI or agentic component. If AI features such as no-show prediction or smart slot suggestions are added later, they get their own plan, with PHI guardrails and a human approval step built first (§7).\n\n## 7. Deliberately deferred\n- **Re-architecting to services, or a UI rewrite.** Pull forward only if the monolith can't meet post-migration SLOs, or release speed blocks clinical requests. Never during the migration.\n- **DB engine change (e.g. SQL Server/Oracle → PostgreSQL).** Pull forward if licensing cost passes the agreed threshold, and run it as a separate project after Phase 6.\n- **Active-active multi-region.** Pull forward only if the hospital network's availability target can't be met by warm cross-region DR. Single-writer stays the rule.\n- **Cloud-native autoscaling and serverless reminders.** Pull forward if Phase 3 load tests or post-cutover peaks show sustained capacity pressure.\n- **New patient self-scheduling or FHIR APIs.** Pull forward after Phase 6, once the cloud has been the stable system of record for at least 90 days.\n- **Migrating adjacent systems (EHR, integration engine as a whole, billing).** Pull forward per system, each with its own dependency-first plan, after this migration is decommissioned.\n- **AI features (no-show prediction, overbooking optimization).** Pull forward when a clinical sponsor and a data-governance approval exist.\n\n## 8. Eval score: 19/20\n\n| # | Dimension | Score | Note |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Dependency ordering | 2 | Data parity → integrations → reads → rehearsal → writes → DR → decommission. Each phase relies on the one before being proven. |\n| 2 | Walking skeleton first | 1 | A real production request crosses every tier on day zero, but it only proves the **read** path. The write path can't be exercised until cutover because of the single-writer rule, so it is first proven in Phase 4 staging rehearsals. This is the weakest dimension. |\n| 3 | Tradeoff gates | 2 | 11 gates, each with a default and a flip condition. \"Without downtime\" is defined honestly as a held write lasting seconds, not literal zero. |\n| 4 | Blast-radius ordering | 2 | Inventory and indirection come before CDC tuning; the singleton guard before dry-runs; read-your-writes handling before the ramp; the patient portal last. |\n| 5 | Security threaded | 2 | The BAA comes before any PHI lands in Phase 0, a pen test comes before real traffic, and there are concrete moves in every phase. |\n| 6 | Observability day zero | 2 | Correlation IDs, lag, and diff are on the dashboard in Phase 0, and every phase adds its own signal. |\n| 7 | Reproducibility | 2 | IaC from the first commit, runbook as code, and staging rebuilt from a masked production clone. |\n| 8 | Resilience | 2 | Fallback in every phase. Classification\n- **What:** Moving a live, in-house (or customizable) patient scheduling application and its relational database from on-prem to a HIPAA-eligible cloud. The system has HL7 links to the EHR, ADT feeds, reminder vendors, and reporting, and it must never visibly go down.\n- **Type:** Infra plus software. This is a data-migration and traffic-routing problem. It is not a rewrite.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness, meaning no lost or double-booked appointments. Compliance (HIPAA) is a close second, and availability is the third requirement.\n- **Worst failure:** Split-brain writes. On-prem and cloud both accept bookings during cutover, which causes double-booked OR or clinic slots, or appointments that silently disappear. A close second is outbound feeds firing twice, which sends duplicate SMS reminders to patients and duplicate SIU messages to the EHR.\n- **Assumptions to confirm before Phase 0:**\n  - **Vendor product?** If the system is a vendor product such as Epic Cadence or Oracle Health scheduling, the vendor's hosting program decides the migration path, and most of this plan becomes vendor-managed.\n  - **What \"without downtime\" means here:** no user-visible outage. The single write cutover still pauses writes for a few seconds (target under 30 s): they are held and then replayed, not rejected. The existing paper downtime procedures stay staffed as a safety net.\n\n## 2. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Default (chosen now) | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Consistency vs availability** | **CP, one writer.** Exactly one database is authoritative at any moment. No dual-writes, no multi-master. The cloud copy is read-only until the cutover. | **Never flip to multi-master for this system.** If availability drills fail RTO, add a cross-region warm standby. It stays single-writer. |\n| **Cutover granularity** | **One atomic write-authority switch for the whole system**, with writes held at the proxy. Shared resources (radiology rooms, surgeons, interpreters) cross department lines, so splitting writes by department would need bidirectional replication. | Flip to per-site cutover only if the Phase 1 inventory proves that a site's resources share nothing with the others. |\n| **Migration style (rehost / replatform / re-architect)** | **Replatform.** Same app code on cloud VMs or containers, with a managed DB on the **same engine** (e.g. SQL Server on-prem → Azure SQL MI or RDS SQL Server). No refactoring during the move. | Flip to rehost (lift-and-shift VMs) if licensing or OS dependencies block managed services. Re-architecting is deferred (§7). |\n| **DB engine change** | **Keep the same engine.** Same-engine CDC is far more reliable, and an engine change on top of a migration compounds risk. | Revisit after migration only if licensing cost is over budget. That becomes its own project. |\n| **Monolith vs services** | **Keep the monolith as-is.** | Extract a service (e.g. reminders) only after migration, if it limits scaling or release speed. |\n| **Sync vs async** | **Synchronous** booking writes, so the user sees a confirmed slot. **Async** CDC replication and interface fan-out over durable queues. | If replication lag p99 goes above 5 s, reads that need fresh data stay on the primary and are not served from the replica. |\n| **Build vs buy** | **Buy:** managed CDC (AWS DMS / Azure DMS / Qlik / GoldenGate), managed DB, and the existing integration engine (Rhapsody / Mirth / Cloverleaf) rehosted. **Build:** only the reconciliation checks and the cutover runbook. | Build trigger-based capture only if the CDC tool can't handle specific types (LOBs, computed columns) or the change volume. |\n| **Cloud / compliance boundary** | A provider with a **signed BAA**, an in-country region, multi-AZ, private connectivity only, and customer-managed keys. | A data-residency or state-law requirement forces the region choice. A provider refusing a BAA disqualifies it. |\n| **Identity** | **Federate to the existing hospital AD** (Entra ID / SAML). No new user store. | None. A second identity store for clinical staff is not acceptable. |\n| **Rollback model** | **On-prem stays a hot standby** after cutover, fed by reverse CDC (cloud → on-prem), for 30–90 days. | Retire it early only after the cloud cross-region DR has passed a failover test. |\n| AI gates (RAG vs fine-tune, hosted vs self-host) | N/A. The migration has no AI component. | Becomes relevant if AI features such as no-show prediction are proposed later (§7). |\n\n## 3. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n**The one real request:** a scheduler looks up *\"provider availability for Clinic X tomorrow.\"* It is served end-to-end from the cloud using real production data. Writes are not possible on this path.\n\n**Tiers crossed:**\n1. Scheduler workstation (existing client, SSO via hospital AD)\n2. On-prem reverse proxy / load balancer (F5 or NGINX). This becomes **the routing control point** for the whole migration.\n3. Redundant private link: ExpressRoute or Direct Connect, plus a backup IPsec VPN\n4. Cloud private load balancer and WAF\n5. Cloud app instance in **read-only mode**, enforced by a database login that only has `SELECT` grants\n6. Cloud managed DB replica, fed by CDC from the on-prem primary. To start, only the tables needed for this one query are replicated.\n\nThe response goes back along the same path.\n\n**Who gets real responses:**\n- 100% of matching requests are mirrored in shadow mode, and the cloud response is diffed against the on-prem response.\n- A pilot group of 3–5 IT or scheduling super-users gets the cloud response for real, using a feature flag at the proxy.\n- If the cloud path is slower than 2 s or errors, the proxy falls back to on-prem.\n\n**Day zero deploy, logging, monitoring:**\n- Infra and app deploy from Terraform/Bicep through a CI pipeline. Nothing is set up by hand.\n- A correlation ID is attached at the proxy and logged on both sides. Logs are structured and PHI-scrubbed, and sent to a SIEM covered by the BAA.\n- The dashboard shows p95 latency, error rate, CDC lag, shadow-diff rate, and proxy fallback count. Alerts go to on-call.\n- **Started now because it needs a long lead time:** passive network-flow and DB-connection capture on the on-prem DB server, so monthly and quarterly jobs show up in the Phase 1 inventory.\n\n**Exit check:**\n- A pilot user's availability lookup returns from the cloud in production.\n- The trace shows every tier, and the lag and diff metrics are visible on the dashboard.\n- The shadow-diff rate is 0 over 72 h, apart from known differences that are explained.\n\n## 4. Phases (ordered by dependency; within a phase, widest blast radius first)\n\n**Phase 0: Walking skeleton** (above)\n- Tasks, in order:\n  1. BAA signed\n  2. Landing zone with policy guardrails\n  3. Private connectivity\n  4. SSO federation\n  5. Proxy routing control point\n  6. Partial CDC\n  7. Read-only app instance\n  8. Dashboard\n\n**Phase 1: Prove the data substrate and find every dependency**\n- Unlocks: everything else. Nothing gets routed to the cloud until the data is provably identical and every consumer is known.\n- Depends on: the Phase 0 CDC path and private link working in production.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Dependency inventory.** Combine flow capture, DB login audit, interface-engine routes, and cron/SQL Agent jobs to list every reader and writer: ADT inbound, SIU outbound, reminder/IVR vendor, billing, reporting/BI, and ODBC links from Access or Excel. A missed consumer is the most likely silent failure after cutover.\n  2. **Put indirection in front of every consumer.** Every client, interface, and report must reach the system through the proxy or a DB listener/DNS alias. The cutover then becomes a routing change instead of reconfiguring 40 clients. Remove hardcoded IPs.\n  3. **Full-database CDC** with schema parity checks. Schema changes are frozen, or applied to both sides through versioned migrations.\n  4. **Continuous reconciliation:** hourly row counts plus per-table checksums, and a nightly full-hash comparison of the appointment and slot tables.\n  5. Restore a cloud backup to a scratch instance to prove point-in-time recovery (PITR) works.\n- Exit check:\n  - 14 consecutive days of full replication with lag p99 under 5 s and zero unexplained reconciliation diffs.\n  - The inventory is signed off by the interface team and department leads.\n  - 100% of consumers go through switchable indirection.\n\n**Phase 2: Rebuild integrations in the cloud, in dry-run**\n- Unlocks: moving traffic without breaking feeds to the EHR, billing, and patients.\n- Depends on: the Phase 1 inventory, plus replicated data that is proven identical.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Write-authority flag and singleton guard.** A single flag says which side is authoritative. Every outbound interface and batch job (reminders, SIU, nightly exports) checks it before acting, so the cloud **cannot** send to patients or to the EHR while on-prem is authoritative.\n  2. Run cloud outbound interfaces in **capture-only mode**. Generated HL7 SIU and reminder payloads are compared message-by-message with what on-prem actually sent.\n  3. Pre-provision the inbound ADT path to the cloud, but leave it inactive. On-prem still receives ADT, and the changes reach the cloud through CDC.\n  4. Re-point reports and BI to the cloud replica, since they only read.\n- Exit check:\n  - 7 days of outbound dry-run with a 100% match against on-prem messages.\n  - The singleton guard is verified by trying to fire a cloud job while on-prem is authoritative. It must refuse.\n  - Reports run from the cloud without a regression.\n\n**Phase 3: Move read traffic gradually**\n- Unlocks: proven cloud capacity and latency under real load before writes depend on it.\n- Depends on: Phase 2 interfaces running in parallel, and the Phase 1 reconciliation staying green.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Handle read-your-writes.** After a user writes, route that session's reads to the primary for 30 s. Also, if CDC lag goes over the threshold, the proxy sends all reads to on-prem automatically.\n  2. Load-test the cloud at 2× the observed peak, for example the Monday 08:00 booking surge.\n  3. Ramp read routing through the proxy: 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%, department by department, with automated canary analysis at each step.\n  4. Move portal \"view my appointments\" to the cloud last, because it is patient-facing.\n- Exit check:\n  - 100% of reads served from the cloud for 14 days with SLOs met (p95 under 800 ms, errors under 0.1%).\n  - The stale-read counter stays at 0 complaints and 0 detected cases.\n\n**Phase 4: Rehearse the write cutover and the rollback**\n- Unlocks: a cutover whose risk has been measured, not guessed.\n- Depends on: Phase 3 proving the cloud can carry production load.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Reverse CDC** (cloud → on-prem), built and verified in staging. This is the rollback mechanism.\n  2. **Cutover runbook as code:** the scripted sequence with go/no-go checks at every step.\n  3. **At least 3 full rehearsals and at least 1 full rollback rehearsal** on a staging environment built from IaC, using a masked clone of production data at production size. Time each one.\n  4. Define rollback triggers. Examples: booking error rate above 0.5% for 5 min, any double-booking detected, interface ACK failures, or CDC reverse lag above 60 s.\n  5. Get clinical operations sign-off. Choose a low-volume window (e.g. Sunday 02:00, avoiding month-end and holidays). Put downtime procedures and print-ready schedules on standby.\n- Exit check:\n  - The rehearsed write-hold is under 30 s, three times in a row.\n  - The rollback rehearsal restores on-prem authority in under 15 min with zero data loss.\n  - The CAB and the CMIO sign off.\n\n**Phase 5: Switch write authority**\n- Unlocks: the cloud becomes the system of record.\n- Depends on: a Phase 4 rehearsal passing at the current production versions.\n- Tasks, executed from the rehearsed script:\n  1. The proxy holds writes, with a bounded queue.\n  2. Confirm CDC lag is 0 and checksums match.\n  3. Set the on-prem DB to read-only.\n  4. Flip the write-authority flag.\n  5. Start reverse CDC.\n  6. Activate cloud ADT inbound, outbound interfaces, and batch jobs. The singleton guard turns on-prem's copies off.\n  7. Release the held writes to the cloud.\n  8. Run synthetic book/cancel transactions against a test patient.\n  9. Hold a **4-hour war-room watch**, then a 72 h heightened watch.\n- Exit check:\n  - 72 h with zero double-bookings, zero lost appointments (reconciled against reverse CDC), all interface ACKs green, and SLOs met.\n\n**Phase 6: Bake, prove DR, decommission**\n- Unlocks: retiring on-prem without losing the safety net it currently provides.\n- Depends on: a stable Phase 5 cloud primary.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Cross-region DR replica plus a real failover test.** On-prem is the only DR until this passes, so it comes first.\n  2. Keep the on-prem hot standby for 30–90 days.\n  3. Make on-prem a read-only archive and apply record-retention rules.\n  4. Decommission with NIST 800-88 media sanitization certificates.\n  5. Close out on-prem accounts, firewall rules, and circuits.\n- Exit check:\n  - The DR failover test meets RTO ≤ 1 h and RPO ≤ 5 min (targets to confirm with clinical ops).\n  - The decommission certificates are filed.\n\n## 5. Cross-cutting concerns (per phase, from the first commit)\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **0** | BAA signed; landing-zone policy guardrails; private endpoints only; CMK encryption; TLS 1.2+; AD federation; read-only DB login | Correlation IDs on both sides; PHI-scrubbed logs to SIEM; latency, error, lag, and diff dashboard; on-call alerts | All infra in Terraform/Bicep through CI; immutable app images; no console changes | Proxy falls back to on-prem on timeout or error; dual circuits plus VPN backup; the cloud path is shadow/pilot only |\n| **1** | Least-privilege CDC service account; replication over the private link only; HIPAA risk assessment updated; DB access audit logging | Reconciliation and lag metrics with SLO alerts; inventory dashboard of every consumer | Schema as versioned migrations; CDC task config in git; reconciliation queries in git | Multi-AZ cloud DB; CDC resumes from checkpoint; tested PITR restore |\n| **2** | Interface credentials in a secrets manager; HL7 over TLS/VPN; vendor endpoints allow-listed | Message-level outbound diff dashboard; interface ACK/NAK monitoring | Interface-engine routes exported to git; the write-authority flag defined in code | Durable queues with DLQs; singleton guard prevents duplicate sends; replayable message store |\n| **3** | WAF rules tuned; **external pen test before any real user traffic beyond the pilot**; portal session security reviewed | Per-route SLOs; canary analysis per ramp step; stale-read counter | Routing rules and flags as code; load-test scripts versioned | Automatic read fallback on lag or latency breach; 2× peak load test passed |\n| **4** | Access review of every cutover operator; tabletop of a PHI incident during cutover | Cutover single-pane dashboard; synthetic book/cancel probes every minute | Runbook as code; staging rebuilt from IaC with a masked production clone; rehearsal timings recorded | Reverse CDC verified; rollback rehearsed under 15 min; downtime procedures and printed schedules staged |\n| **5** | Just-in-time privileged access for the cutover window only; every cutover action logged to the SIEM | War-room dashboard; continuous double-booking detector query; interface ACK alarms | Cutover runs from the rehearsed, version-pinned script; change freeze in effect | Bounded write-hold queue; predefined rollback triggers; hot on-prem standby through reverse CDC |\n| **6** | Revoke on-prem accounts and firewall rules; NIST 800-88 sanitization; retention policy applied | DR replication lag monitoring; cost and capacity dashboards; post-migration SLO report | DR environment built from the same IaC; as-built documentation generated from code | Cross-region failover tested; scheduled game days; standby retired only after DR passes |\n\n## 6. AI layer\nN/A. This plan has no AI or agentic component. If AI features such as no-show prediction or smart slot suggestions are added later, they get their own plan, with PHI guardrails and a human approval step built first (§7).\n\n## 7. Deliberately deferred\n- **Re-architecting to services, or a UI rewrite.** Pull forward only if the monolith can't meet post-migration SLOs, or release speed blocks clinical requests. Never during the migration.\n- **DB engine change (e.g. SQL Server/Oracle → PostgreSQL).** Pull forward if licensing cost passes the agreed threshold, and run it as a separate project after Phase 6.\n- **Active-active multi-region.** Pull forward only if the hospital network's availability target can't be met by warm cross-region DR. Single-writer stays the rule.\n- **Cloud-native autoscaling and serverless reminders.** Pull forward if Phase 3 load tests or post-cutover peaks show sustained capacity pressure.\n- **New patient self-scheduling or FHIR APIs.** Pull forward after Phase 6, once the cloud has been the stable system of record for at least 90 days.\n- **Migrating adjacent systems (EHR, integration engine as a whole, billing).** Pull forward per system, each with its own dependency-first plan, after this migration is decommissioned.\n- **AI features (no-show prediction, overbooking optimization).** Pull forward when a clinical sponsor and a data-governance approval exist.\n\n## 8.
